title: Buck, Boost & Buck-Boost
description: Conversion ratios, currents and voltage stresses of the three basic converters, sizing L and C, and how inductor resistance limits gain and efficiency.

study.title: Explore: three basic converters
study.body: The same switch, diode and inductor, arranged three ways, give three conversion ratios (CCM, ideal parts). The **buck** steps down, $M = D$. The **boost** steps up, $M = 1/D'$. The **buck-boost** inverts the polarity and can step up or down, $M = -D/D'$. Drag $D$ to compare.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& M_{buck} = D\\ & M_{boost} = \frac{1}{1 - D}\\ & M_{buck\text{-}boost} = -\frac{D}{1 - D}\end{aligned}

study.title: The buck-boost converter
study.body: $Q_1$ on: the inductor is charged from the input ($v_L = V_g$) while the diode blocks and $C$ feeds the load. $Q_1$ off: the inductor current continues through the diode and pulls the output **negative** ($v_L = V$). Volt-second balance: $DV_g + D'V = 0$. The load current only arrives during $D'T_s$, so $I_L = |I_{out}|/D'$.

study.title: DC currents and component stresses
study.body:
- **Buck**: $I_L = I_{out}$; $Q_1$ and $D_1$ block $V_g$.
- **Boost**: $I_L = I_{in} = I_{out}/D'$; $Q_1$ and $D_1$ block $V$.
- **Buck-boost**: $I_L = I_{out}/D'$; $Q_1$ and $D_1$ block $V_g + |V|$.
In all three the switch carries $i_L$ during $DT_s$ (average $DI_L$) and the diode during $D'T_s$ (average $D'I_L$); both see the peak $I_L + \Delta i_L$.

study.title: Sizing L and C
study.body: Choose the inductor ripple first, typically $2\Delta i_L$ = 20–40 % of $I_L$, and solve for $L$. Then choose $C$ for the allowed output ripple: in the buck the capacitor only sees the inductor ripple; in the boost and buck-boost it must supply the whole load current while $Q_1$ is on, so they need much more capacitance.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& 2\Delta i_L = \frac{V_gDT_s}{L}\quad\text{(boost, buck-boost)}\\ & 2\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_g - V)DT_s}{L}\quad\text{(buck)}\\ & 2\Delta v = \frac{I_{out}DT_s}{C}\quad\text{(boost, buck-boost)}\end{aligned}

study.title: Inductor copper loss: the DC transformer model
study.body: Put the winding resistance $R_L$ in series with the inductor. Volt-second balance then contains an extra $-I_LR_L$ in each interval. The result is an ideal **DC transformer** with ratio $1 : M(D)$ plus the resistor $R_L$. For the boost the model is $V_g$, $R_L$ and a $D' : 1$ transformer; referred to the output, $R_L$ looks like $R_L/D'^2$, so the loss grows quickly at large $D$.

study.title: Explore: boost with copper loss
study.body: With $R_L$ the boost gain no longer goes to infinity: it peaks at $M_{max} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{R_L/R}}$ at $D' = \sqrt{R_L/R}$ and falls beyond, while the efficiency collapses. For the buck the same analysis gives $V = DV_g/(1 + R_L/R)$ and $\eta = 1/(1 + R_L/R)$; for the buck-boost, $\eta$ has the same form as for the boost. Drag $R_L/R$.

study.title: Worked example: boost with copper loss

steps.title: The buck-boost converter
steps.body: Move the inductor to the switch node and the diode to the output and you get the buck-boost. While $Q_1$ is on the inductor charges from $V_g$; while it is off the inductor discharges into the output through the diode, making the output **negative**. Volt-second balance: $DV_g + D'V = 0$.

steps.prompt: A buck-boost converter runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}}. Find the output voltage (with sign).
steps.explanation: $V = -\frac{D}{1 - D}V_g$ = −{{D}}/{{1-D||2}} × {{Vg}} V = **{{-Vg*D/(1-D)|V}}**. For $D$ < 0.5 the magnitude is below $V_g$, above 0.5 it is larger.

steps.prompt: A buck-boost converter must make −{{Vo|V}} from {{Vg|V}}. What duty cycle does it need?

steps.title: Comparing M(D)
steps.body: The buck ratio is linear in $D$. The boost and buck-boost ratios grow without bound as $D \to 1$ (in theory: losses limit them in practice). Drag $D$ and compare the three readouts.

steps.prompt: Match each conversion ratio to its converter
steps.explanation: Buck: on $v_L = V_g - V$, off $-V$. Boost: on $V_g$, off $V_g - V$. Buck-boost: on $V_g$, off $V$. Volt-second balance on each gives the three ratios.

steps.prompt: A sensor needs −12 V, and the only supply is a 5 V rail. Which basic converter can do this with one inductor?
steps.explanation: Only the buck-boost inverts the polarity, and with $D$ = 12/(12 + 5) = 0.71 it also steps the magnitude up. The buck and boost keep the output positive.

steps.prompt: A boost converter runs from {{Vg|V}}. The curve shows $V$ versus $D$. Move the operating point (dot) to an output of {{k*Vg|V}}.
steps.explanation: $V = V_g/(1 - D)$ → $D = 1 - V_g/V$ = 1 − {{Vg}}/{{k*Vg}} = **{{1-1/k||3}}**. Note how flat the curve is at small $D$ and how steep it gets near 1: a boost is hard to control at high gain.

steps.prompt: An ideal buck-boost converter at $D$ = 0.5 delivers an output voltage of the same magnitude as its input.
steps.explanation: $|M| = D/(1 - D)$ = 0.5/0.5 = 1. The output is $-V_g$: same magnitude, opposite polarity.

steps.title: Where the current flows
steps.body: Charge balance on the output capacitor gives the DC inductor current. In the buck the inductor feeds the output all the time, so $I_L = I_{out}$. In the boost and buck-boost the output is fed only through the diode during $D'T_s$, so $I_L = I_{out}/D'$. The switch and diode share $i_L$: averages $DI_L$ and $D'I_L$.

steps.prompt: A boost converter steps {{Vg|V}} up to {{V|V}} and delivers {{Io|A}}.

ask.prompt: What is the DC inductor current?
ask.explanation: $D' = V_g/V$ = {{Vg/V||3}}. $I_L = I_{out}/D'$ = {{Io|A}} / {{Vg/V||3}} = **{{Io*V/Vg|A}}**. Power balance agrees: $V_gI_L = VI_{out}$.

ask.prompt: What is the average switch current?
ask.explanation: $D = 1 - V_g/V$ = {{1-Vg/V||3}}, $I_L$ = {{Io*V/Vg|A}}. The switch conducts $i_L$ during $DT_s$: $\langle i_Q\rangle = DI_L$ = **{{Io*V/Vg*(1-Vg/V)|A}}**. The diode carries the rest, $D'I_L = I_{out}$ = {{Io|A}}.

steps.prompt: A buck-boost converter makes −{{Vo|V}} at {{Io|A}} from {{Vg|V}}.

ask.prompt: What voltage must the MOSFET block when it is off?
ask.explanation: With $Q_1$ off the diode conducts, so the switch node sits at the output, −{{Vo}} V, while the MOSFET's other side is at +{{Vg}} V. It blocks $V_g + |V|$ = **{{Vg+Vo|V}}**. The diode blocks the same voltage when $Q_1$ is on.

ask.prompt: What is the DC inductor current?
ask.explanation: $D = \frac{|V|}{|V| + V_g}$ = {{Vo/(Vo+Vg)||3}}, $D'$ = {{Vg/(Vo+Vg)||3}}. $I_L = I_{out}/D'$ = {{Io|A}} / {{Vg/(Vo+Vg)||3}} = **{{Io*(Vo+Vg)/Vg|A}}**: the sum of input ({{Io*Vo/Vg|A}}) and output current.

steps.prompt: A boost converter makes {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}}. What voltage must its MOSFET and diode be able to block (before adding margin)?
steps.explanation: $Q_1$ off: the diode conducts and the switch node sits at $V$ = {{V|V}}, so the MOSFET blocks $V$. $Q_1$ on: the switch node is at 0 and the diode blocks $V$. Both need a rating above **{{V|V}}**.

steps.title: Choosing L and C
steps.body: Pick the inductor ripple (20–40 % of $I_L$ peak-to-peak is typical) and solve the ripple formula for $L$. For the output capacitor: a buck's $C$ only filters the inductor ripple, but in a boost or buck-boost $C$ alone carries the load for $DT_s$, so it must be much larger for the same ripple. The formulas below are for the boost and buck-boost, where $v_L = V_g$ while $Q_1$ is on (for a buck, replace $V_g$ by $V_g - V$ in $L$).

steps.prompt: A boost converter: {{Vg|V}} → {{V|V}} at {{Io|A}}, $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. Choose $L$ for a peak-to-peak inductor ripple of {{r*100}} % of $I_L$.
A buck-boost converter delivers {{Io|A}} at $D$ = {{D}} and $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. What output capacitance gives {{dv|V}} peak-to-peak ripple (ignore ESR)?
steps.explanation: While $Q_1$ is on, $C$ alone supplies {{Io|A}} for $DT_s$ = {{D/fs|s}}. $C = \frac{I_{out}DT_s}{2\Delta v}$ = {{Io|A}} × {{D/fs|s}} / {{dv|V}} = **{{Io*D/(fs*dv)|F}}**.

steps.prompt: A buck converter delivers {{Io|A}} at $D$ = {{D}}.

ask.prompt: What is the average MOSFET current (= average input current)?
ask.explanation: In the buck $I_L = I_{out}$. The MOSFET carries it during $DT_s$: $DI_L$ = {{D}} × {{Io|A}} = **{{D*Io|A}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the average diode current?
ask.explanation: The diode carries $I_L = I_{out}$ during $D'T_s$: $D'I_L$ = {{1-D||2}} × {{Io|A}} = **{{(1-D)*Io|A}}**. At low $D$ (large step-down) the diode carries most of the current, which is why synchronous rectifiers pay off there.

steps.title: The DC transformer model
steps.body: Include the inductor winding resistance $R_L$ and redo volt-second balance: each interval gets an extra $-I_LR_L$. The converter then behaves like an ideal $1 : M(D)$ DC transformer with $R_L$ in series. For the boost (shown), $R_L$ referred to the output is $R_L/D'^2$.

steps.prompt: A buck converter runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} into $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. The inductor has $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}; everything else is ideal.

ask.explanation: Volt-seconds with $I_L = V/R$: $D V_g - I_LR_L - V = 0$ → $V = \frac{DV_g}{1 + R_L/R}$ = {{D*Vg|V}} / (1 + {{RL/R||3}}) = **{{D*Vg/(1+RL/R)|V}}**.
The same current flows through $R_L$ and $R$, so $\eta = \frac{R}{R + R_L} = \frac{1}{1 + R_L/R}$ = 1 / (1 + {{RL/R||3}}) = **{{100/(1+RL/R)|%}}**.

steps.prompt: A boost converter runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} into $R$ = {{R|Ω}}; the inductor has $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}.
A boost converter has $R_L/R$ = {{a}}. The curve shows its gain $M$ versus $D$. Set $D$ for the **largest** output voltage.
steps.explanation: $M = \frac{D'}{D'^2 + R_L/R}$ is largest where $D' = \sqrt{R_L/R}$ = √{{a}} = {{sqrt(a)||3}}, so **$D$ = {{1-sqrt(a)||3}}** and $M_{max} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{R_L/R}}$ = {{1/(2*sqrt(a))||3}}. Beyond this point more duty cycle only adds loss: the controller must never go there.

steps.prompt: A buck-boost converter runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} into {{R|Ω}}; the inductor resistance is {{RL|Ω}}.
A non-synchronous buck converter makes {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}}. Its diode drops {{VD|V}}; the MOSFET and inductor are ideal.

ask.explanation: Off-interval: $v_L = -V - V_D$. Volt-seconds: $D(V_g - V) - D'(V + V_D) = 0$ → $V = DV_g - D'V_D$ → $D = \frac{V + V_D}{V_g + V_D}$ = {{V+VD}} / {{Vg+VD}} = **{{(V+VD)/(Vg+VD)||3}}** (ideal: {{V/Vg||3}}).

$D$ = {{(V+VD)/(Vg+VD)||3}}. Input current is $DI$, so $\eta = \frac{VI}{V_gDI} = \frac{V}{DV_g}$ = {{V}} / ({{(V+VD)/(Vg+VD)||3}} × {{Vg}}) = **{{100*V/(Vg*(V+VD)/(Vg+VD))|%}}**. Equivalent: $\eta = \frac{V}{V + D'V_D}$: the diode drop hurts most at low output voltage.

steps.prompt: With a real inductor (winding resistance), a boost converter can still reach any output voltage by pushing $D$ close enough to 1.
steps.explanation: $M = \frac{D'}{D'^2 + R_L/R}$ peaks at $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{R_L/R}}$ and falls to zero as $D \to 1$: the inductor current $V/(D'R)$ grows so large that $R_L$ eats all the voltage. With $R_L/R$ = 0.01 the boost cannot exceed 5×.

steps.prompt: A boost converter takes {{Vg|V}} and delivers {{Po|W}} at {{V|V}}. How much power does its {{RL|Ω}} inductor resistance dissipate? (Use the ideal duty cycle and current.)
steps.explanation: The inductor carries the input current: $I_L = P/V_g$ = {{Po/Vg|A}}. $P_{Cu} = I_L^2R_L$ = ({{Po/Vg|A}})² × {{RL|Ω}} = **{{(Po/Vg)^2*RL|W}}**. Low-voltage, high-power boosts need very low-resistance inductors.

steps.prompt: Design a boost converter: {{Vg|V}} → {{V|V}} at {{Io|A}}, $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}, peak-to-peak inductor ripple 30 % of $I_L$, output ripple {{dv|V}} peak-to-peak.

ask.explanation: $I_L$ = {{IL|A}}, $\Delta i_L$ = half of {{pp|A}} = {{pp/2|A}}. The switch carries $i_L$ while on, up to $I_L + \Delta i_L$ = **{{1.15*IL|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A synchronous buck converter (two MOSFETs, each {{Ron|Ω}}) with an inductor of {{RL|Ω}} runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} into {{R|Ω}}.

ask.explanation: In both intervals the inductor current flows through one MOSFET and $R_L$: $D V_g - I(R_{on} + R_L) - V = 0$ with $I = V/R$, so $V = \frac{DV_g}{1 + (R_{on} + R_L)/R}$ = {{D*Vg|V}} / (1 + {{(Ron+RL)/R||3}}) = **{{D*Vg/(1+(Ron+RL)/R)|V}}**.
The load current sees $R_{on} + R_L$ = {{Ron+RL|Ω}} in series all the time: $\eta = \frac{R}{R + R_{on} + R_L}$ = **{{100*R/(R+Ron+RL)|%}}**.

steps.prompt: A boost converter runs at $D$ = {{D}} into $R$ = {{R|Ω}} with an inductor resistance of {{RL|Ω}}. What is its efficiency?
steps.explanation: $I_L = V/(D'R)$, so the copper loss relative to the output power is $\frac{I_L^2R_L}{V^2/R} = \frac{R_L}{D'^2R}$ = {{RL/((1-D)^2*R)||3}}. $\eta$ = 1/(1 + {{RL/((1-D)^2*R)||3}}) = **{{100/(1+RL/((1-D)^2*R))|%}}**. $1/(1 + R_L/R)$ is the buck result, where $I_L = I_{out}$.

steps.prompt: A battery-powered boost converter delivers {{Po|W}} at {{eta*100}} % efficiency. The battery voltage sags to {{Vb|V}} near the end of discharge. What average current does the converter draw from the battery then?
steps.explanation: $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$ = {{Po|W}} / {{eta}} = {{Po/eta|W}}. $I_{in} = P_{in}/V_b$ = {{Po/eta|W}} / {{Vb|V}} = **{{Po/(eta*Vb)|A}}**. The inductor and switch must be rated for this worst case (plus ripple), not for the nominal battery voltage.

steps.prompt: A boost converter's inductor has $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} and the load is {{R|Ω}}. What is the highest voltage gain $V/V_g$ it can reach?
steps.explanation: $M = \frac{D'}{D'^2 + R_L/R}$ is largest at $D' = \sqrt{R_L/R}$ = {{sqrt(RL/R)||3}}: $M_{max} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{R_L/R}}$ = 1 / (2 × {{sqrt(RL/R)||3}}) = **{{1/(2*sqrt(RL/R))||3}}**. At that point the efficiency is only 50 %.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of designing a CCM DC–DC converter in order
items: Choose the topology from the input and output voltages
Calculate the duty-cycle range from M(D)
Find the DC inductor current from charge balance
Choose the ripple and calculate L
Calculate C from the output ripple spec
Check peak currents, voltage stresses and losses
steps.explanation: The topology fixes $M(D)$; $D$ and the DC currents follow from the balance equations; the ripple specs then size $L$ and $C$; finally the peak currents and blocking voltages select the semiconductors, and the losses tell you whether the efficiency target is met.

steps.prompt: For the same load current, switching frequency and output voltage ripple (and a typical 20–40 % inductor ripple), a boost converter needs more output capacitance than a buck converter.
steps.explanation: In the buck the capacitor only absorbs the small triangular inductor ripple. In the boost the diode current is pulsed: during $DT_s$ the capacitor alone supplies the full load current, so $C = I_{out}DT_s/(2\Delta v)$, typically far more.
